titre: Translating a contract into Swiss law: what legal quadrilingualism changes
auteur: Legal and linguistic team at Neur.on
extrait: The federal laws are in German, French and Italian, and the three versions are authoritative. Specific consequences for a contract: abbreviations that change according to language, English without legal force, fake friends between Italian from Switzerland and Italian, and a method of checking in three minutes.
bref: In Switzerland, the terminology of a contract is not a matter of style. The laws are published in German, French and Italian, and all three versions are authoritative. The translator therefore does not seek an equivalent: he reproduces the one already adopted by the legislator.
title: Translating a contract into Swiss quadrilingual law · Neur.on
description: Laws published in three languages, abbreviations that change, English without legal force: what Swiss quadrilingualism imposes on a translated contract.

titre: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, Pitche at EPFL Investor Day 2024
extrait: Three minutes on stage and an unexpected tip received in masterclass: remove the team slide. Paula Reichenberg put it into practice in the afternoon for a more relaxed and hopefully more convincing pitch.
bref: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, visited EPFL Investor Day, the largest investor event in French-speaking Switzerland. Before going on stage, she attended a pitch Masterclass moderated by Jordi Montserrat. She found one unexpected tip: remove the slide from the team, because the energy generated on stage counts more.
title: Paula Reichenberg at EPFL Investor Day 2024 · Neur.on
description: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, visited EPFL Investor Day, the largest investor event in French-speaking Switzerland, with unexpected advice.
court: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, Pitche at EPFL Investor Day 2024
corps:
What to remove from your pitch deck when you only have 3 minutes on stage?

before going on stage, all participants were invited to attend a masterclass dedicated to pitch, moderated by one of the most brilliant minds in this field, Jordi Montserrat.

One of his remarks really surprised Paula. The discussion was about what to get out of his pitch when he does n't stick to the time limit. There was general agreement that the 5-year roadmap or financial data could legitimately go into the trap.

But Jordi said: remove the team.

the team? The backbone of the company in terms of expertise and personality? It ca n't go to potential investors.

But Jordi's reasoning was clear: “on stage, you embody the energy of your company. If it's good, it's worth more than the team slide.”

and you know what? Paula applied this advice to her afternoon pitch. She gained 2 to 3 breathing breaks, for a more relaxed presentation and (hopefully) more convincing.

She knows that she does n't give up her team. After all, when faced with interested investors, it never takes him 3 minutes to start exhausting himself on his co-founders and team.

titre: Key insights from the LegalTechTalk 2024 conference in London
extrait: “I refuse to pay for information I already have.” Legal Directors and law firms exchanged views on trust, effectiveness and the role of technology in legal services.
bref: Neur.on reports on the discussions at the LegalTechTalk 2024 conference in London. Legal directors advocated a relationship of trust and knowledge sharing with their external law firms. The firms highlighted tailor-made teams, data-based process analysis and their role as technology advisors, including legal translation.
title: Legaltechtalk 2024 in London: key lessons · Neur.on
description: Neur.on explains the lessons learned from LegalTechTalk 2024 in London: expectations of legal directors, trust with law firms and the role of LegalTech.
court: Key insights from the LegalTechTalk 2024 conference in London
corps:
What do the legal directors of their law firms expect?

“I refuse to pay for information I already have,” says the legal director of an energy company, asked about his main criteria for commissioning external law firms.

“This is a simplistic view,” and certainly not a solid basis for building a sustainable and fruitful relationship with referenced law firms, "says the legal director of a multinational company, who manages the legal functions of more than 15 countries. “If you expect a firm to bring directly applicable added value and operational advice, corporate lawyers and external lawyers need to share their knowledge and build common ground. This requires investment and trust on both sides.”

“confident” is not the first adjective that comes to mind to describe attorneys: they have been trained to stay safe and skeptical to better protect their customers. Changing posture is not self-evident, says a head of legal innovation at a law firm.

“They must understand that legal directors do not always expect guaranteed accuracy: obtaining their most informed opinion in urgent cases is the priority, and forecasts that prove to be false are part of business life. Giving the firms you referenced clear information about the type and volume of work that they can expect from your company also helps build trust: if lawyers can invest enough to understand your business and expectations, they will propose solutions on their own to increase efficiency."

How do law firms organize themselves to meet them?

“When we work with legal directors, our lawyers' goal is to act as an extension of their team," says Innovation Director of a law firm in continental Europe. “When a new client arrives, our priority is to find contacts whose working and communication style matches that of the legal director. To address each of its issues, we then set up ad hoc teams that bring together the right mix of business expertise, training paths and seniority levels.”

Why does technology become a deliverable of law firms?

“in addition to the right team, data-based process analysis is essential to efficiently provide legal services,” adds Jordan Lee, Chief Strategy Officer of Pogust Goodhead, a law firm specializing in collective appeals. “As soon as you identify an automated step or repetitive patterns that can be streamlined, the technical team can intervene and even capture the smallest marginal gains. When overcome, they quickly lead to significant savings and higher quality."

“There is a clear trend: clients expect their lawyers to act as technology advisors as soon as possible. For example, in the area of Neur.on expertise, clients confronted with major translation challenges in a legal case expect their lawyers to have an economical and secure solution at their disposal. Testing, benchmarking and co-creation of LegalTech tools are now among the deliverables of law firms.”

Some lessons from the conference. Make a note of next year's edition on your diaries! Thank you very much to Bradley Collins, Charlotte Johnstone and Merlin Beyts for this brilliant organization.

titre: Should AI startups fear the AI Act? The lessons of the Grand challenge
extrait: Eight AI solutions look at the draft AI Act: Neur.on learns three lessons from this, including a low-cost compliance lever for startups with tight finances.
bref: Representatives of Neur.on, iCoSys and CertX participated in the first major challenge of the University of St. Gallen on the EU AI Act. They assessed the compliance of 8 AI solutions with the draft regulation. According to Neur.on, AI risk awareness and a compliance culture provide a lot of value without significant expenditure.
title: Should start-ups fear the AI Act? · Neur.on
description: In 2023, Neur.on, iCoSys and CertX evaluated 8 AI solutions with respect to the AI Act project at the Grand challenge of the University of St. Gallen.
court: Should AI startups fear the AI Act? The lessons of the Grand challenge
corps:
What was the Grand challenge of the University of St. Gallen on the AI Act?

We had the honour to see representatives of Neur.on, iCoSys and CertX, alongside other renowned AI experts from around the world, participate in the First University of St. Gallen Grand challenge: The EU AI ACT. At this event, we focused on assessing the compliance of 8 leading AI solutions with the current AI Act project. These solutions covered robotics, process management and NLP analytics. Our team, with diverse profiles, brought together experts in ISO 27001 machine learning, law and certification.

Click here to find out more in the Swiss national television journal!

should AI startups fear the AI Act?

here are our main lessons:

  • the fundamental principles of the EU IA Act (including human action and control, technical robustness and security, privacy and data governance, transparency, diversity, non-discrimination and fairness, and social and environmental impact) are well designed, found fair and essential to build widely shared acceptance and trust in artificial intelligence.
  • However, for financially tense start-ups, complying with the requirements of the AI Act may be akin to a sword of Damocles, consuming resources and slowing development.
  • Fortunately, as we noted during the Grand challenge, one aspect of compliance does not require significant expenses but provides considerable value: AWARENESS of AI risks and a CORPORATE CULTURE that prioritizes compliance and responsible growth.

We will work together for an AI industry that embraces compliance, responsible development and a culture of trust.

Thank Thomas Burri for organizing such a spectacular challenge, thank SRF (Schweizer Radio und Fernsehen) for covering the event, and thank all our team members: Jean Hennebert, Orane Laeri, Yael Iseli, Arman Iranfar and Marco Repetto Ph. D.

titre: Neur.on at the GEN AI Summit 2024 in Lausanne: the challenges of AI in legal translation
extrait: Why do tools like DeepL have problems with specialist legal and financial texts? At the GEN AI Summit 2024, the CEO of Neur.on discussed the nuances between legal systems, cultural barriers and the future of AI in translation.
bref: On 29 May 2024, Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, attended the GEN AI Summit 2024 in Lausanne at the Domain Specific Innovation session. She outlined the limitations of tools such as DeepL for specialist legal and financial translations, the cultural and linguistic challenges of legal translation and the expected progress of AI in this area.
title: GEN AI Summit 2024 Lausanne: AI and translation · Neur.on
description: On 29 May 2024, Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, spoke at the GEN AI Summit in Lausanne about the limitations of automatic translation.
court: Neur.on at the GEN AI Summit 2024 in Lausanne: the challenges of AI in legal translation
corps:
the GEN AI Summit 2024 in Lausanne brought together industry leaders and innovators to shape the future of technology. We are proud to announce that our CEO, Paula Reichenberg, was among the speakers at the summit on 29 May. She shared her view of the dynamic world of generative AI.

at the summit, discussions went beyond the big ads from tech giants like OpenAI and Google. Participants were able to explore various cases of use with panoramai.ch. These examples showed the real value of generative AI and gave participants concrete paths for their own projects.

Paula participated in the Domain specific Innovation session, together with renowned speakers such as Raphael Briner, Pascal Wicht, Romain Rosay (CTO of AMPLIFY) and Deepak Tewari (CEO of Privately). This session explored the subtleties of AI and technology in their own projects. different sectors.

key points of Paula's intervention

  • limits of current automatic translation tools: Paula highlighted the difficulties of using tools such as DeepL for specialized legal and financial translations. She stressed the difficulty of distinguishing between different legal systems.
  • Cultural and linguistic challenges: She mentioned the important cultural and linguistic barriers that make it difficult to obtain accurate translations, an essential issue in legal context.
  • future ambitions of AI in legal translation: Paula presented progressive improvements and future objectives of AI to better serve the field of legal translation.

wider impact of AI

the session also addressed broader societal impacts of AI, including possible job losses and ethical challenges of AI applications. Public issues have raised concrete problems, such as precision in age detection by ethnic origin or in the management of deepfakes. Panellists reassured the public of ongoing efforts to refine these technologies and ensure their compliance with regulatory standards.

Look at the full discussion.

titre: Neur.on among the 4 finalists of the Swiss FinTech Awards 2024

description: Neur.on, the SaaS platform for translation by AI, is one of the 4 finalists of the Swiss FinTech Awards 2024. Final on 11 June in Rüschlikon.
court: Neur.on among the 4 finalists of the Swiss FinTech Awards 2024
corps:
NEUR.ON is one of the 4 finalists of the Swiss FinTech Awards 2024.

You think there is an error?

“But how could SaaS translation platform powered by IA be considered a FinTech?”, you may ask yourself. Especially if you met us during the countless LegalTech events in which we participated.

the jury of the Swiss FinTech Awards nevertheless understood that accurate terminology and convincing wording far exceed the legal realm.

titre: LegalTech and lawyers, allies or competitors? Lessons from the digital study day
extrait: Most LegalTech tools want to serve lawyers, not compete with them. However, their adoption remains difficult. Fit to work processes, intuitive interface and responsive customer service: three keys to success.
bref: The founder of Neur.on took part in the “LegalTech” round table of the Digital study Day organised by the Latin Conference of Baskers on 29 September 2023. His finding: the key to the success of a LegalTech tool is its ease of use, with intuitive interface, alignment to lawyers' processes and responsive customer service.
title: LegalTech and lawyers: allies or competitors? · Neur.on
description: At the LegalTech Roundtable held by the Latin Conference of Buttoners in 2023, the founder of Neur.on explains why simple usage takes precedence.
court: LegalTech and lawyers, allies or competitors? Lessons from the digital study day
corps:
contrary to what some lawyers might fear, most of the LegalTech tools created in recent years are designed to serve legal professionals rather than compete with them. However, there are as many disappointed LegalTech entrepreneurs as lawyers who complain about the inadequacy of the new tools offered to them.

How to connect LegalTech startups with legal professions?

the need to create a bridge between innovative startup fervor and the specific needs of the professions under the aegis of Vinciane Gillet, the Bulgarian bar was persuaded to establish a tailor-made incubator. In Switzerland, we need the support of the Swiss LegalTech Association and the commitment of some cutting-edge studies, which accept responsibility for co-creation with LegalTech and invest the time and resources needed to test new tools (thanks to them).

This was one of the topics discussed at the “LegalTech” round table on the day of the digital study organized by the Latin Conference of Bastonners, I was pleased to attend together with Vinciane Gillet (GILLET-LEX), Ariel Ben Hattar (Lenz & Staehelin) and Camille Auberson (Approovd).

What is the key to the success of a legal technology tool?

interrogated by Juliette Ancelle (ID is lawyers) and Stéphanie Chuffart-Finsterwald (sigma legal) on lessons learned as a LegalTech entrepreneur founder of NEUR.ON, I would say that the key to the success of a legal technology tool is its ease of use. The overburdened schedules of lawyers leave no room for technical training “in anticipation of future needs”. For example, the legal translation requirements of a study vary greatly from year to year, so out-of-context training for assistants or trainees to a translation tool would be a waste of time. The solutions must therefore be intuitive and logical enough for the lawyer to be able to achieve the expected result from the first use, within a few clicks, or to call upon a responsive customer service to fill any “ad hoc” knowledge gaps.

to conclude with a rather easy play on words, the masters of words for a solution adapted to the masters' hands are therefore:

  • fit with the work processes of lawyers, without any ambition to change them;
  • intuitive interface, not requiring any prior training;
  • Customer Service, including professional hours and emergency situations

titre: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, is part of the Female Founder Project 2025 of UBS

corps:
It is said that the founders receive other questions. our CEO Paula Reichenberg has other answers.

According to the Harvard Business Review, among the many, complex and mysterious reasons why women obtain much less venture capital (1.8% of total venture capital in 2024), describes how questions are asked to founders during fundraising.

concurrently, 67% of the questions asked to entrepreneurs are promotion-oriented (hopes, achievements, progress), while 66% of the questions asked to entrepreneurs are prevention-oriented (safety, responsibility, potential risks).

What is that changing? If we do not know these patterns, we invariably answer them in the statement of reasons for the question. For a woman, this may give a more conservative and more risk-averse image, and therefore a less interesting investment opportunity.

being a woman, Paula “does n't care”. Nor does its zodiac sign. She never complains that the world is unfair and does not waste time seeing herself as the victim of anything. She does her best with the cards she has in her hand.

But this requires getting prepared, whether at fundraising or in any other professional situation. It therefore thanks UBS for including it in this year's Female Founder program. This is a modern approach to speeding up founders' success, through a comprehensive investor readiness program.

She hopes that this preparation will involve a lot of really tricky questions.

titre: Geneva International legal week 2025: a panel on profitable AI with Paula Reichenberg

corps:
are the high initial costs of AI integration really only “training costs”?

This is at least described, euphemistically, by some innovators of leading law firms and legal departments.

But for anyone who knows their budget, you need a clear indication that AI improves its return on investment.

You may have heard it a hundred times over the past 24 months: using AI maximises productivity, improves the quality of your work and reduces the risk of legal consequences and delays. It can also generate much more profit while making the legal system accessible to more people.

What you may not have heard is HOW to achieve this.

titre: Commercial register of Schwyz: extracts translated into English by the Neur.on IA
extrait: Hundreds of people requested a reliable English translation of an extract every month from the Schwyz commercial register. Back to a project that originated in Sandbox innovation in the canton of Zurich, and the pitfalls of Swiss legal concepts.
bref: The commercial register of the Canton of Schwyz offers English translations of its extracts produced by AI, which no other canton offers. Neur.on has developed the translation model through the innovation Sandbox for Artificial Intelligence of the Canton of Zurich. DV Bern AG, Head of zefix.ch, was responsible for implementation on the authorities side.
title: Schwyz: extracts from the register translated by AI · Neur.on
description: Schwyz is the only canton whose commercial register offers translation of extracts into English by AI, with a model developed by Neur.on.
court: Commercial register of Schwyz: extracts translated into English by the Neur.on IA
corps:
the canton of Schwyz is a pioneer in AI.

the commercial register of Schwyz now offers what no other canton offers: of the extracts translations into English made by AI.

Schwyz is not only the pittoresque cradle of Switzerland, to which he gave his name. The canton has also introduced a very pragmatic AI application for companies based in its territory.

How did the draft extract translation come about?

previously, hundreds of people called the Schwyz commercial register each month with one and the same request: “I need a reliable English translation of an extract. Could you please help me?"

Othmar Aeschi of the Handelsregister Schwyz, known for its leading role in innovation, had the informed intuition that AI could help. He contacted Raphael von Thiessen, Economic Promotion Division of Amt für Wirtschaft, Kanton Zürich. Raphael incorporated this challenge into the Federal Office's Sandbox for Artificial Intelligence innovation and NEUR.ON in connection with the Schwyz commercial register. and we developed the most accurate translation model for this specific use. on the part of the authorities, the project was then implemented with the support of DV Bern AG, the specialised it company responsible for the commercial registry's online platform, zefix.ch.

Why are Swiss legal concepts difficult to translate into English?

the challenge was not just about automatic language processing engineering. The more important question was how to accurately translate typical Swiss legal concepts into English, avoiding misunderstandings (or even misunderstandings) in cross-border relations.

  • Prokurist
  • Kollektivunterschrift zu zweien
  • Gesellschafter (einer GmbH vs. einer Kommanditgesellschaft)?
  • Streichung vs. Löschung?
  • Stimmrechtsaktien vs. Vorzugsaktien?

If you have already wondered how to correctly translate each of these terms into its context, you know how far a poor translation can fall from the target.

Cerise on the cake for lawyers-linguists, we were also able to address epicenic translations, particularly for functions on the Board of Directors which 50 years ago were occupied exclusively by men.

as you can see, cutting-edge AI projects require, in order to succeed, a broad human expertise in the field.

who contributed to the project?

a warm thank you all project stakeholders, in particular for the countless hours invested by Othmar Aeschi of the Handelsregister Schwyz, Raphael von Thiessen of the Amt für Wirtschaft, as well as Thierry Coita and Michael Gillmann of DV Bern AG. Also thank you to Carmen Walker Späh for tireless support to Zurich Innovation.

titre: Trust Valley 2023: Cyber security and data sovereignty – a sustainable Swiss tradition?
extrait: Legal translation projects are a weak, often neglected, link in data security. At the invitation of Trust Valley, Neur.on shares the findings of a panel on SMEs and asks about a Swiss sandbox at CHF 2.5 million.
bref: Neur.on took part in a panel at the Trust Valley Day at the Rolex learning Center at EPFL in 2023. The panel focused on the pressure of digital security on SMEs and start-ups. Neur.on reported on the demand from its customers: a 100% Swiss infrastructure, not subject to the CLOUD act, to test generative AI.
title: Data sovereignty in Switzerland: Trust Valley · Neur.on
description: At the Trust Valley Day 2023 at EPFL, Neur.on spoke about the data security of SMEs and reported on the call for 100% Swiss infrastructure.
court: Trust Valley 2023: Cyber security and data sovereignty – a sustainable Swiss tradition?
corps:
the day of the Trust Valley at the Rolex learning Center at EPFL brought together actors from politics, academia, cybersecurity and the private sector, in particular SMEs, to discuss concrete challenges facing our country's economy.

NEUR.ON serves as law firms, Swiss banks and public administrations. It responds to one of their weakest links in terms of data security (Yes, drafts for legal translation represent a significant but often overlooked risk!). Lennig Pedron therefore kindly invited us to share our experience as a LegalTech start-up that places digital security at the heart of its business.

What pressure does digital security put on SMEs?

These are some of the key findings of the panel dedicated to the pressure on SMEs and start-ups:

  • cutting edge digital security requires substantial investment: infrastructure, processes, documentation and above all an up-to-date corporate culture, shared at all levels and across all services. The total is often six-digit per year.
  • Law firms and other SMEs outside the ICT sector often lack the resources and skills needed to correctly assess the security level of their suppliers. They only have to “trust” or “hope everything goes well”.
  • specialised ICT providers, such as Neur.on, can handle certain specific stages of the process, but the SME remains responsible for overall knowledge and vigilance.
  • programs and associations such as Trust4SMEs, the Swiss AI Center for SMEs of HES-SO University of applied Sciences of Western Switzerland and the Swiss LegalTech Association are there to help, with guides, white papers and training.

requested by Swiss SMEs from the public sector?

However, the main message from our clients and LegalTech stakeholders is addressed to the Swiss public sector and innovation programmes:

Swiss SMEs and start-ups look forward to exploring the potential of generative AI for their industry. They must be able to use their own data with LLMs without fear of data leakage or uncontrolled data flows. They urgently require 100% Swiss infrastructure, not subject to the US CLOUD Act or Patriot Act, to safely test different technologies.

who is willing to help raise the CHF 2.5 million needed for a Swiss SME sandbox?

is Switzerland ready to play a role in the race for digitisation?

Join Neur.on in its commitment to the safety and success of Swiss companies on this path.

titre: MIDS 2023 conference in Geneva: Paula Reichenberg on the adoption of generative AI
extrait: More than 200 lawyers and referees gathered for the 15-year Master in International dispute Settlement. Alongside Professor Jacques de Werra, Paula Reichenberg has combined generative AI with automatic translation.
bref: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, was a panellist at the 3 rd Alumni Conference of the Master in International dispute Settlement (MIDS) in Geneva in September 2023. The event celebrated the 15 th anniversary of the program and brought together more than 200 arbitration specialists. Paula Reichenberg compared the adoption phases of generative AI and automatic translation.
title: MIDS 2023 conference in Geneva: General AI · Neur.on
description: In Geneva in September 2023, Paula Reichenberg (Neur.on) compared the adoption of generative AI with the adoption of automatic translation at the age of 15 of MIDS.
court: MIDS 2023 conference in Geneva: Paula Reichenberg on the adoption of generative AI
corps:
Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, and Professor Jacques de Werra, eminent in contract and intellectual property law at the Faculty of Law of the University of Geneva and Director of the Digital Law Center of Geneva, were panelists at the 3 rd Alumni Conference of the renowned Master in International dispute Settlement (“MIDS”) program. It was held in Geneva in September 2023.

This event brought together more than 200 arbitration lawyers and arbitrators from around the world to discuss key aspects of the settlement of international disputes and strengthen links within the enlarged MIDS community. This year's edition was of particular importance, as it celebrated the 15 th anniversary of the MIDS program.

Paula Reichenberg and Professor Jacques de Werra took part actively as panellists, while the discussion was moderated brilliantly by Sean McCarthy, Consultant in International Arbitration.

Paula's interventions focused on the phases of adoption of generative AI and their remarkable parallels with the phases of adoption of generative AI. automatic translation over the past five years.

titre: Paula Reichenberg, CEO and founder of Neur.on, named “Digital shaper 2023” by BILANZ
extrait: This award belongs to the entire team. Neur.on sees it as an opportunity to recall three beliefs about the digitisation of law: technology for lawyers, transparency and human expertise.
bref: Paula Reichenberg, CEO and founder of Neur.on, was named Digital shaper 2023 by BILANZ Wirtschaftsmagazin, digitalswitzerland, SME, HANDELSZEITUNG and Innosuisse. Neur.on attributes this award to the commitment of her entire team. The company advocates the digitisation of law that respects the work of lawyers, relies on transparency and values human expertise.
title: Paula Reichenberg, Digital aper 2023 · Neur.on
description: Paula Reichenberg, CEO and founder of Neur.on, is named Digital shaper 2023 by BILANZ, digitalswitzerland, SME, HANDELSZEITUNG and Innosuisse.
court: Paula Reichenberg, CEO and founder of Neur.on, named “Digital shaper 2023” by BILANZ
corps:
This award demonstrates the remarkable commitment and collaborative spirit of the entire Neur.on team.

in the field of digital shaping, success is the result of a collective effort. This is particularly true in the legal sector, where the principles of trust, accuracy and ethics take precedence over temporary concepts such as profitability, entrepreneurial risk … and sometimes innovation.

at Neur.on, we are convinced that true digitisation succeeds when:

  • Technology strengthens without crushing: our approach is to align the technology in a fluid manner with the working methods and professional requirements of lawyers. It is about harmonizing innovation with the essence of legal practice, without imposing unnecessary changes.
  • transparency is the cornerstone: we are committed to the principle of transparency. We do not engage in holistic vantage and instead provide lawyers with accurate information on the reliability of our results. Honest information enables them to act knowingly.
  • Human expertise is enhanced: if technology is a powerful ally, it can never replace the depth and depth of human expertise. We defend the role of lawyers, who know how to navigate in complexity, and recognize that no algorithm can replicate their nuanced understanding of diverse situations.

together, we commit to transforming our industry to bring joy to all its stakeholders.

titre: BDÜ 2022 conference: Paula Reichenberg on cooperation between lawyers and translators
extrait: The right translations are based on open communication between lawyers and translators. Back to a round table discussion at the BDÜ conference, and on everyone's expectations of automatic translation.
bref: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, took part in a roundtable discussion on working in and with law firms at the BDÜ e. V. conference in 2022. She stressed that lawyers expect translators not to deny the potential of automatic translation, and that translators want lawyers not to overestimate it.
title: Conference BDÜ 2022: lawyers and translators · Neur.on
description: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, took part in a roundtable discussion at the BDÜ conference on work in and with law firms in 2022.
court: BDÜ 2022 conference: Paula Reichenberg on cooperation between lawyers and translators
corps:
Paula Reichenberg, our CEO, had the privilege of participating in a panel discussion on working in and with law firms at the conference on BDÜ e. V.- die qualifizierten Dolmetscher und Übersetzer, alongside Karen Rückert and Dirk Poppendieck. The discussion was moderated by Richard Delaney.

for Karen, the main lesson of the panel is: “Good translations are the result of open communication between lawyers and translators. But that does n't mean lawyers have to read in their minds. Translators must have sufficient confidence to ask the right questions, in order to obtain the information necessary for a translation tailored to their purpose. And they have to ask them so that lawyers understand why it's worth spending time answering them. Translators and lawyers need to meet at the interface of law and language, so that clients get the service they want and need.”

Paula added to this synthesis that lawyers expect translators not to deny the potential of automatic translation, while translators would want lawyers not overestimate it.
